options.A: Remaining dose is 28 Gy over the 19 fractions still to come
options.B: Remaining dose is 52 Gy over the 19 fractions still to come
options.C: Remaining dose is 38 Gy over the 14 fractions still to come
options.D: Remaining dose is 38 Gy over the 19 fractions still to come

explanation: The correct answer is D (Remaining dose is 38 Gy over the 19 fractions still to come): Dose per fraction is 66 ÷ 33 = 2 Gy. Delivered so far is 14 × 2 = 28 Gy, so remaining is 66 minus 28 = 38 Gy over 33 minus 14 = 19 fractions. Check: 19 × 2 = 38 Gy. Giving 28 Gy reports what has already been delivered, and 52 comes from subtracting 14 fractions from 66 Gy.

question: A physicist compares a hypofractionated plan of 40 Gy in 15 fractions with conventional treatment for a tumour with an α/β of 10 Gy. Using BED = n × d × (1 + d ÷ (α/β)) with d about 2.67 Gy, which tumour BED is correct?

options.A: About 50.7 Gy, worked out as 40 Gy × (1 + 2.67 ÷ 10)
options.B: About 3.4 Gy, worked out as 2.67 Gy × (1 + 2.67 ÷ 10)
options.C: About 75.6 Gy, worked out as 40 Gy × (1 + 2.67 ÷ 3)
options.D: About 40 Gy, worked out as 40 Gy × (1 + 0 ÷ 10)

explanation: The correct answer is A (About 50.7 Gy, worked out as 40 Gy × (1 + 2.67 ÷ 10)): With n × d = 40 Gy and an alpha beta of 10 Gy, BED = 40 × (1 + 2.667 ÷ 10) = 40 × 1.2667 = 50.7 Gy. Using an alpha beta of 3 Gy gives 75.6 Gy, which is the late responding tissue figure rather than the tumour. Leaving out the number of fractions gives about 3.4 Gy. BED equals the physical dose only when dose per fraction is negligible, which is not so for 2.67 Gy fractions.

question: A planner in Sydney proposes changing a 50 Gy course from 25 fractions of 2 Gy to 20 fractions of 2.5 Gy to save time, keeping the same total. He says the tumour will do better. A colleague asks what happens to a late responding tissue with α/β of 3 Gy.

options.A: Tumour BED rises more than late tissue BED, so the schedule is safer overall
options.B: Late tissue BED stays the same because the total dose is unchanged at 50 Gy
options.C: Late tissue BED rises from about 83 to 92 Gy, so total dose needs lowering
options.D: Late tissue BED falls, because fewer fractions give fewer chances to damage normal cells

explanation: The correct answer is C (Late tissue BED rises from about 83 to 92 Gy, so total dose needs lowering): For late tissue with α/β of 3 Gy, 25 fractions of 2 Gy give 50 × (1 + 2 ÷ 3) = 83.3 Gy, while 20 fractions of 2.5 Gy give 50 × (1 + 2.5 ÷ 3) = 91.7 Gy. That is about a 10 percent rise. The tumour with α/β of 10 Gy rises only from 60 to 62.5 Gy, about 4 percent, so a hypofractionated schedule needs a lower total dose.

question: A man on a 30 fraction radical prostate course in Wollongong missed three consecutive treatment days with gastroenteritis and returns on Monday feeling well. The booking system shows he could still finish a week late. His records show no instruction about the gap.

options.A: Treat as scheduled and record nothing, since a short break does not matter
options.B: Treat as scheduled, then report the interruption to the radiation oncologist to decide compensation
options.C: Refer him straight to the dietitian because gastroenteritis counts as a treatment toxicity
options.D: Add an extra fraction on Saturday to make up the missed days

explanation: The correct answer is B (Treat as scheduled, then report the interruption to the radiation oncologist to decide compensation): Missed or interrupted fractions allow tumour cells to repopulate, so the therapist reports the gap to the radiation oncologist, who decides how to compensate. Quietly adding an extra treatment or ignoring the gap are the common wrong choices. His illness was not caused by radiation, so a toxicity referral does not fit.

question: A woman in week 3 of breast radiotherapy has red, itchy skin and asks what she can do. She has used the same perfumed body cream for years and likes washing with hot water. Which advice is most appropriate? The nurse is busy with another patient.

options.A: Wash gently in lukewarm water with mild soap, pat dry, and use approved moisturisers
options.B: Wash gently in lukewarm water, pat dry, and keep using her usual perfumed cream
options.C: Cover the area with a waterproof adhesive dressing to protect it from rubbing on clothing
options.D: Wash gently in lukewarm water, pat dry, and apply any pharmacy cream before each treatment

explanation: The correct answer is A (Wash gently in lukewarm water with mild soap, pat dry, and use approved moisturisers): Advice is to wash gently with lukewarm water and mild soap, pat dry, and use only moisturisers the department approves. Gentle washing with her perfumed cream is half right but the cream may irritate reacting skin. Applying any pharmacy cream before treatment is also unsafe because products on the skin can change the dose and irritate. Adhesive dressings pull on reacting skin.

question: In week 4 of breast treatment, a patient in Cairns has moist peeling skin in the fold under her breast. She says she is coping and would rather keep going than 'make a fuss'. Her next fraction is due in ten minutes.

options.A: Continue treatment and write the reaction in the chart for the weekly review only
options.B: Reassure her that this is expected and will settle once the course finishes
options.C: Report the moist peeling today so the nurse can assess it and approve a dressing
options.D: Advise her to keep the fold dry with talc and monitor it at her next review

explanation: The correct answer is C (Report the moist peeling today so the nurse can assess it and approve a dressing): Moist peeling in a skin fold is a significant acute reaction that needs assessment and a department-approved dressing, so it is reported the same day. Waiting for a weekly review or recommending talc leaves the skin unprotected. Reassurance is kind and partly true, because it will heal, but it does not meet her needs now.

question: A head and neck patient in Hobart, in week 4, has lost 3 kg since last week and says even water is painful to swallow. He insists he is fine and wants his treatment done quickly because his partner is waiting outside.

options.A: Weigh him again at the next weekly visit and suggest softer foods meanwhile
options.B: Record the weight loss in the notes and mention it at next week's review
options.C: Advise extra oral nutrition supplements and note the weight at the next visit
options.D: Tell the nurse or radiation oncologist the same day and request dietitian review

explanation: The correct answer is D (Tell the nurse or radiation oncologist the same day and request dietitian review): A 3 kg loss in a week with painful swallowing suggests mucositis, which needs a same day report and dietitian review because he may need a feeding tube. Documenting it for next week's review delays care. Supplements and softer foods are sensible advice but do not replace escalation. His wish to hurry does not change what must be reported.

question: After a lecture on acute reactions, a student asks the therapist to define xerostomia, which she has seen in the notes of several head and neck patients. Which description is correct? The notes for these patients mention reduced saliva, altered taste and painful swallowing as separate problems.

options.A: Pain or difficulty when swallowing food and fluids, which often leads to weight loss
options.B: Altered taste sensation that comes on during the course of treatment and can persist
options.C: Soreness and ulcers affecting the lining of the mouth and throat during treatment
options.D: Dry mouth from reduced saliva when the salivary glands lie within the treated volume

explanation: The correct answer is D (Dry mouth from reduced saliva when the salivary glands lie within the treated volume): Xerostomia is dry mouth caused by reduced saliva after the salivary glands receive dose. Mucositis is the sore ulcerated lining, altered taste is a separate effect, and painful swallowing is a consequence of mucositis. They often occur together, which is why they are easy to confuse.

question: A man having prostate radiotherapy in Adelaide has been told to follow a bladder filling routine before each treatment. He asks why it matters, as he finds it uncomfortable. Which explanation is most accurate? He has already emptied his bladder twice today and is worried about being late.

options.A: It displaces small bowel upward out of the beam, which is the only reason
options.B: It keeps bladder size and position reproducible, so the treated volume matches the plan each day
options.C: It reduces bladder movement from breathing, so the prostate stays still during beam on
options.D: It lowers the risk of urinary infection by flushing the urethra before each fraction

explanation: The correct answer is B (It keeps bladder size and position reproducible, so the treated volume matches the plan each day): A set bladder filling routine keeps the size and position of the bladder, and so the prostate region, close to the planning scan, so the treated volume matches the plan. Bowel displacement can occur but is not the main purpose. Breathing has little effect on the pelvis, and the routine does not prevent infection. Explaining the reason often helps patients put up with the discomfort.

question: A woman having radical pelvic radiotherapy in Brisbane with weekly cisplatin tells you she had six loose stools yesterday and cramping overnight. She says the nurse told her diarrhoea is normal and she would like to just get on the couch.

options.A: Report the diarrhoea today, because chemotherapy can strengthen reactions and she may need review
options.B: Hold her treatment until stools settle, since combined therapy makes radiation unsafe
options.C: Assume it is the usual bowel reaction and note it for the weekly review
options.D: Encourage fluids and loperamide from her own supply, then treat normally

explanation: The correct answer is A (Report the diarrhoea today, because chemotherapy can strengthen reactions and she may need review): Some diarrhoea is expected, but six stools with cramping while having concurrent chemotherapy is a strengthened reaction, so it is reported the same day. The nurse's earlier reassurance does not cover a change since then. Deciding to hold treatment belongs to the oncologist.

question: A first-year student asks which acute side effect is the most common overall in people having radiation therapy, regardless of treatment site, and what helps. The therapist wants the single most accurate statement. She has seen skin, mouth and bowel reactions this week and wants a statement that holds across sites.

options.A: Mucositis, which affects most patients treated to the head and neck
options.B: Fatigue, which builds over the weeks and is helped by rest and pacing
options.C: Nausea, which develops in many patients having treatment to the head
options.D: Skin erythema, which appears in most patients treated near the surface

explanation: The correct answer is B (Fatigue, which builds over the weeks and is helped by rest and pacing): Fatigue is the most common side effect overall, builds over the weeks, and is helped by rest, gentle activity and pacing. Skin reactions, nausea and mucositis are common but depend on the treated site. The question asks for the most common effect across all patients.

question: A man in Perth on radical lung radiotherapy and immunotherapy arrives with a new itchy rash on his chest, a dry cough that is worse than last week, and two loose stools this morning. He says 'it's probably just the radiation'.

options.A: Attribute the rash to a radiation skin reaction and give skin care advice only
options.B: Tell him to raise it with his medical oncologist at his appointment next month
options.C: Report the new symptoms to the radiation oncologist or nurse promptly before treating
options.D: Treat as planned, since breathlessness is expected in lung treatment, and mention it at weekly review

explanation: The correct answer is C (Report the new symptoms to the radiation oncologist or nurse promptly before treating): Immunotherapy can cause rash, bowel inflammation and breathlessness, and radiation can produce similar effects, so new symptoms are reported promptly rather than assumed to be routine. Three different new symptoms together need team assessment. Waiting for weekly or monthly reviews leaves a potentially serious problem unseen.

question: A student is asked to describe the difference in timing for acute and late radiation reactions in a patient information session. Which statement is correct? A new patient and her husband have asked what to expect, so the student wants the timeline correct before explaining it to them at the information session.

options.A: Acute reactions appear in fast dividing tissue within three months and are usually permanent
options.B: Acute reactions appear during treatment in slow dividing tissue and usually heal
options.C: Acute reactions appear in the first week only, in skin, and usually heal
options.D: Acute reactions appear during treatment or within about three months and usually heal

explanation: The correct answer is D (Acute reactions appear during treatment or within about three months and usually heal): Acute reactions appear during treatment or within about three months, arise in fast dividing tissue such as skin, mucosa and bowel lining, and usually heal. Late effects arise months to years later in slowly dividing tissue and are often permanent. Mixing the permanence of late effects with acute timing is tempting but wrong. Acute reactions are not limited to the first week or to skin.

question: An oncologist in Melbourne wants to move a chest wall patient to larger daily fractions to shorten the course. The physicist says the total dose must be lowered, not kept the same. A student asks what justifies this. Late heart effects are a concern.

options.A: Late responding tissue is very sensitive to fraction size, so its BED rises more than tumour
options.B: The tumour effect rises faster than the late tissue effect, so a lower total is safer
options.C: Larger fractions reduce repopulation, which pushes acute skin reactions past their limit
options.D: Fewer fractions give normal tissue less oxygen between treatments, making it more radiosensitive overall

explanation: The correct answer is A (Late responding tissue is very sensitive to fraction size, so its BED rises more than tumour): With larger fractions, the late tissue BED (α/β about 3 Gy) rises proportionally more than the tumour BED (α/β about 10 Gy), as shown by 20 percent against 8 percent in the chapter's example. This is why a hypofractionated schedule needs a lower total dose. Late tissue damage is often permanent, so the protection matters most.

question: A three-year-old with a brain tumour is booked for radiotherapy in Sydney. He cannot lie still and his parents are very anxious. The team meets to plan immobilisation and support. Which approach best reflects paediatric principles? The family travelled from the country and has little experience of hospitals.

options.A: Use a mask and parents' reassurance, and avoid anaesthetic because of its risks in toddlers
options.B: Involve a play specialist and parents, and use anaesthetic as the team decides, for safe immobilisation
options.C: Use a tighter rigid mask without sedation so that movement cannot occur
options.D: Start treatment as planned and use sedation given by the therapists on the machine

explanation: The correct answer is B (Involve a play specialist and parents, and use anaesthetic as the team decides, for safe immobilisation): Young children who cannot stay still need comforting immobilisation, a play specialist, parents or carers, and sometimes a general anaesthetic decided by the team. Avoiding anaesthetic altogether may leave a child unable to hold still. A tighter mask without sedation is neither safe nor comforting. Sedation is not given by therapists at the machine, so that plan falls outside their scope.

question: A student is preparing a short talk on children having radiotherapy. She asks the therapist which general principle for treatment volume and dose is correct, given children's growing tissues and long life ahead. She will present to the paediatric team on Friday.

options.A: Give fewer, larger fractions to reduce how often the child needs anaesthetic
options.B: Cover the whole growth region to protect future function, using a moderate dose
options.C: Treat the smallest necessary volume, using the lowest effective dose
options.D: Use the same volume and dose as adults, adjusted only for the child's weight

explanation: The correct answer is C (Treat the smallest necessary volume, using the lowest effective dose): Because children's tissues are still growing and late effects can appear over a long life, the principle is the smallest necessary volume with the lowest effective dose. Covering a whole growth region adds normal tissue to the field. Adult volumes and doses scaled by weight ignore growth. Fewer, larger fractions raise the risk of late effects.

question: A man with prostate cancer and bone metastases arrives for his treatment in Launceston saying he has had a band of pain around his chest since yesterday and his legs 'feel wobbly' when he stands. Today's plan is ready and the machine is free.

options.A: Stop, keep him safe, and report to the radiation oncologist immediately
options.B: Deliver today's fraction since the plan is ready, then report the symptoms afterwards
options.C: Let him wait on the trolley and report to the oncologist after the list
options.D: Advise him to take his usual pain relief and mention it at his review

explanation: The correct answer is A (Stop, keep him safe, and report to the radiation oncologist immediately): Band-like pain with leg weakness in a patient with bone metastases is a warning sign of spinal cord compression, an emergency because paralysis can become permanent. The therapist stops, keeps him safe and escalates at once. Treating first, waiting until the list ends, or waiting for a review all delay care.

question: Four patients are waiting in a busy Perth radiation therapy department just before the morning list. Each has told you about a new or ongoing symptom while you checked their identity. Which one needs the radiation oncologist urgently, before any treatment is delivered, because delay could cause permanent harm?

options.A: A prostate patient with unchanged back ache of three months and normal walking
options.B: A lung cancer patient with new numbness in both feet and trouble passing urine overnight
options.C: A breast patient with moist peeling in a skin fold who is otherwise comfortable and coping
options.D: A head and neck patient with a sore mouth who has lost 1 kg this week

explanation: The correct answer is B (A lung cancer patient with new numbness in both feet and trouble passing urine overnight): New numbness and bladder changes suggest spinal cord compression, which needs immediate escalation because delay can cause permanent paralysis. The skin and mouth reactions are real toxicities that need a same-day report. Unchanged back ache with normal walking is the least urgent of the four.

question: A 62-year-old man with lymphoma in the chest is booked for treatment lying flat in Canberra. Today his face, neck and arms are visibly swollen, his neck veins are distended and he says he cannot breathe lying down. The set-up images are due.

options.A: Ask him to raise his arms above his head, which will ease the swelling
options.B: Position him flat as planned, since reproducibility matters, and report afterwards
options.C: Hold positioning, keep him comfortable, and ask the team before lying him flat
options.D: Lie him flat briefly for set-up images, then sit him up between beams

explanation: The correct answer is C (Hold positioning, keep him comfortable, and ask the team before lying him flat): Facial and arm swelling, distended neck veins and breathlessness on lying flat suggest superior vena cava obstruction. Lying flat may worsen symptoms, so positioning is paused and the treating team is asked first. Plans that rely on the usual position cannot be followed automatically.

question: A patient with known spinal metastases and severe back pain arrives on a trolley in Darwin and must be moved onto the treatment couch. He tells you the pain is worse today and his left leg feels odd. Two therapists are available.

options.A: Pull the sheet quickly with one colleague to shorten his time in pain
options.B: Use a hoist for the transfer and leave reporting to the oncologist's routine review
options.C: Transfer him with the sliding board and the porter, and record the symptom afterwards
options.D: Move him carefully using the department's safe method with help, and report the new leg symptom

explanation: The correct answer is D (Move him carefully using the department's safe method with help, and report the new leg symptom): With spinal metastases and a new leg symptom, the therapist moves the patient carefully using the department's safe method with help and reports the neurological change at once. Pulling the sheet quickly risks further injury. Using equipment is sensible but waiting for a routine review delays care. Handing the move to a porter and recording the symptom afterwards delays the report.

question: A student is shown a high dose rate brachytherapy suite for cervical cancer. She is asked to describe what happens during delivery of the treatment. She has only seen external beam machines before and wants the key difference clearly stated for her notes.

options.A: Staff stay at the bedside holding the applicator steady in the patient while sources decay slowly
options.B: Several low activity sources stay in the applicators for days with staff nursing normally
options.C: A single high activity source is driven from a shielded safe into applicators, then returns
options.D: An X-ray beam is generated and aimed at the applicator from outside the patient

explanation: The correct answer is C (A single high activity source is driven from a shielded safe into applicators, then returns): In HDR treatment, a remote afterloader drives one high activity source out of a shielded safe along guide tubes into the applicators for a few minutes, then returns it. Staff leave the room and watch by camera and intercom. Low dose rate treatment is the one with sources that stay for long periods.

question: A therapist at a Melbourne centre is asked by a student why moving from 1 m to 2 m from a small exposed radioactive source reduces dose so much. Which explanation is correct? She has an exam on protection principles tomorrow.

options.A: Dose rate halves when distance doubles, because it falls in direct proportion to distance
options.B: Dose rate falls with the square root of distance, so doubling distance gives about 70 percent
options.C: Dose rate falls with the cube of distance, so doubling distance gives about one eighth
options.D: Dose rate falls with the square of distance, so doubling distance gives about a quarter

explanation: The correct answer is D (Dose rate falls with the square of distance, so doubling distance gives about a quarter): Radiation from a small source spreads over an area that grows with the square of distance, so doubling the distance leaves about a quarter of the dose rate. A linear relationship would halve it, which is the common first guess. A square root gives a mild fall of about 70 percent, and a cube gives one eighth, which treats spreading as a volume. Both slips give the wrong factor for a point source.

question: During HDR treatment of a cervical patient in Adelaide, the console alarm sounds and shows that the source has not returned to the safe. The patient is conscious on camera. The afterloader's emergency equipment sits in the room. Nobody else has entered the room.

options.A: Press the emergency stop, then enter quickly without a meter to pull out the applicator
options.B: Press the emergency stop, then enter with a survey meter and use emergency equipment
options.C: Reset the console and restart the treatment so that the source retracts by itself normally
options.D: Enter at once with a survey meter and disconnect the guide tube from the afterloader

explanation: The correct answer is B (Press the emergency stop, then enter with a survey meter and use emergency equipment): A source that does not retract calls for the local emergency procedure: press the emergency stop, enter with a survey meter, and use the equipment in the room, which normally includes long forceps and a shielded container. Entering without the stop or without a meter exposes the therapist. Restarting the treatment ignores the fault.

question: After an HDR session in Adelaide, the patient's partner asks if it is safe to hug her, because he has heard she will be radioactive. The source has returned to the afterloader safe and the room survey is complete. He seems frightened.

options.A: Yes, the source is back in the safe, she is not radioactive, so contact is fine
options.B: No, she stays radioactive for about a day, so he should keep a metre away
options.C: Yes, but he should limit close contact for several weeks as with permanent seed implants
options.D: No, she should be isolated until her urine and saliva are checked for contamination

explanation: The correct answer is A (Yes, the source is back in the safe, she is not radioactive, so contact is fine): With HDR brachytherapy the source returns to the shielded afterloader safe, so the patient carries no radioactive material and contact is safe. Precautions for permanent seed implants or unsealed radionuclide therapy are tempting, but they do not apply when no source stays in the body. The room survey confirming the source is in the safe is the evidence the partner needs, and a calm explanation is the right response to his fear.

question: A therapist is preparing a patient for HDR brachytherapy in Brisbane. Before delivery she checks the console. Which set of checks best reflects the practical rules for staff? The physicist is in another room preparing the next plan, and the afterloader is warmed up and ready.

options.A: Check warning lights and interlock, then rely on the afterloader memory for source details
options.B: Check identity, applicator and source details against the prescription, plus lights and interlock
options.C: Check identity only, since the physicist already verified applicator and source details before the session
options.D: Check applicator and source details, and leave the personal monitor on the console

explanation: The correct answer is B (Check identity, applicator and source details against the prescription, plus lights and interlock): Practical rules include confirming identity and the applicator and source details against the prescription, wearing the issued personal monitor, and checking that warning lights and the door interlock work. Relying on others or on memory skips checks that are the therapist's responsibility. Leaving the personal monitor behind or trusting memory for source details are the tempting shortcuts that this question tests.

question: A Vietnamese-speaking man in Sydney is about to receive his side effect explanation before his first treatment. His adult son offers to translate, and says he knows all the medical words. A booking exists for an accredited interpreter. What is the best approach?

options.A: Use a bilingual radiographer from another department who happens to be free
options.B: Use a translation app on a phone and ask the patient to nod if he understands
options.C: Accept the son's help, since he knows his father well and can use plain family words
options.D: Use the accredited interpreter for the explanation, and thank the son for staying

explanation: The correct answer is D (Use the accredited interpreter for the explanation, and thank the son for staying): An accredited interpreter should be used whenever a patient does not speak English well, rather than a family member, especially for consent and clinical information. The son can still stay for support. A translation app or an untrained colleague does not give accuracy or confidentiality.

question: Midway through set-up for a lung patient in Hobart, after the images are taken, he says firmly, 'I can't do this any more, I don't want any more treatment.' The oncologist took his consent two weeks ago and the plan is approved.

options.A: Stop, make him safe, and gently persuade him to reconsider today
options.B: Stop, make him safe, and rebook him for tomorrow without further discussion
options.C: Stop, make him safe, and tell the radiation oncologist
options.D: Stop, make him safe, and tell the nurse to decide about treatment

explanation: The correct answer is C (Stop, make him safe, and tell the radiation oncologist): Consent can be withdrawn at any time, so earlier consent does not oblige him to continue. The therapist stops, makes him safe and informs the radiation oncologist, who holds responsibility for the treatment decision and can talk with him. Persuading him alone, rebooking without discussion or handing the decision to a nurse all skip that step. Each leaves the oncologist unaware of a significant event.

question: An 84-year-old woman in Cairns, newly confused, is about to start treatment. Her daughter says, 'I'm her decision maker, just go ahead.' No paperwork has been shown, and the patient seems unsure what is happening today. The oncologist is in clinic until noon.

options.A: Pause, follow the local process for a substitute decision maker, and inform the oncologist
options.B: Accept the daughter as her decision maker, since families usually speak for older patients
options.C: Assume she lacks capacity and proceed, since treatment is clearly in her best interest today
options.D: Assume she has capacity because she nodded, and carry on with treatment

explanation: The correct answer is A (Pause, follow the local process for a substitute decision maker, and inform the oncologist): If a person may lack capacity, the therapist follows the local process for a substitute decision maker and does not assume. A relative's statement without paperwork is not a substitute for that process, and a nod is not clear evidence of understanding. The radiation oncologist is told so consent can be properly established.

question: An Aboriginal man from a remote community in the Northern Territory has travelled several hundred kilometres from Country for treatment in Darwin. At his first session he is quiet, avoids eye contact and asks if his brother can sit with him. The schedule is tight.

options.A: Arrange a quiet room and an interpreter, then proceed with the standard process unchanged
options.B: Ask his brother to sign the consent paperwork on his behalf to save time
options.C: Explain the process briefly, then ask him to tell staff if he has concerns
options.D: Offer a liaison officer if available, allow time and family, and ask openly about his needs

explanation: The correct answer is D (Offer a liaison officer if available, allow time and family, and ask openly about his needs): Cultural safety means the patient decides whether care feels safe, so staff offer support, allow time and family presence, and ask openly. An Aboriginal liaison officer, where available, helps with this after a long journey from Country. Assuming a language need, handing decisions to his brother or leaving him to raise concerns each replaces asking with an assumption. Those options fall short even though each looks considerate.

question: A woman receiving pelvic radiotherapy in Adelaide asks for a female therapist for her set-up because of her faith and modesty. Today's roster has two male therapists on her bunker and one female therapist in another bunker. The department prides itself on person-centred care.

options.A: Proceed with the male therapists and offer a gown, since draping covers modesty
options.B: Explain that therapists are allocated by roster and cannot be changed
options.C: Ask her openly about her needs and arrange a female therapist where possible within safe practice
options.D: Delay all her treatment until a female therapist is rostered to her sessions

explanation: The correct answer is C (Ask her openly about her needs and arrange a female therapist where possible within safe practice): Cultural safety includes asking openly about modesty, religion and the gender of the practitioner, and adjusting within safe practice. Swapping with the female therapist in the other bunker is a reasonable adjustment. Refusing, assuming, or delaying her whole course each fail to balance her needs with safe care.

question: In week 4 of treatment, a woman in Brisbane says while changing, 'Everyone would be better off without me.' She seems flat and her fraction is due in five minutes. The department has a nurse on the floor. Her partner is waiting outside.

options.A: Stay with her, take it seriously, and escalate to the nurse or oncologist the same day
options.B: Reassure her, record the comment in her notes, and raise it at the weekly review
options.C: Treat her on time to protect routine, then report the comment to the nurse afterwards
options.D: Ask whether she is safe, accept her answer, and note it in the record

explanation: The correct answer is A (Stay with her, take it seriously, and escalate to the nurse or oncologist the same day): A statement suggesting self harm is taken seriously and escalated the same day, and the therapist stays with the patient until the right person takes over. Recording the comment for a later review, treating first, or accepting a quick reassurance all delay help for a person who may be at risk. Documentation matters, but it does not replace immediate escalation to the nurse or oncologist.

question: A newly diagnosed patient in Melbourne is given skin care instructions by a therapist. The therapist wants to check the patient has understood them. Which method best fits the communication guidance in the chapter? She has limited health literacy and is worried about doing it wrong.

options.A: Ask 'Do you understand?' and proceed when she says yes
options.B: Ask her to explain the instructions back in her own words, and provide written information
options.C: Repeat the instructions slowly in the same words, once more
options.D: Hand her a printed leaflet and ask her to read it before her next visit

explanation: The correct answer is B (Ask her to explain the instructions back in her own words, and provide written information): The guidance is to use plain language, explain each step, check understanding by asking the patient to say it back in her own words, and give written information. A bare yes may not reveal confusion, a leaflet alone is not a check, and repetition does not test understanding. Her limited health literacy in the stem is the detail that makes a simple yes unreliable.

question: A planning meeting in Perth discusses a large 8 cm lung tumour with a necrotic, poorly perfused centre. A student asks why the centre is likely to be harder to control with X-rays. Which explanation is most accurate? The student is revising for the registration exam.

options.A: High oxygen tension there prompts repair of double strand breaks before division
options.B: Hypoxic cells there need about two and a half to three times the dose
options.C: Low blood supply there stops radiation reaching it, so the dose delivered is lower
options.D: Cells there divide slowly, so late effects of the treatment appear years afterwards

explanation: The correct answer is B (Hypoxic cells there need about two and a half to three times the dose): Large tumours often have hypoxic centres, and hypoxic cells are about two and a half to three times harder to kill with low LET radiation, the oxygen enhancement ratio. Radiation reaches the whole volume regardless of blood supply, so the dose is not lower. The issue is the cell's sensitivity, not the dose delivered.

question: Two patients are on the same machine in Sydney: one with stage I disease on a six-week radical course and one with stage IV disease on a short palliative course. A student asks why their plans differ so much and why stage matters to a therapist who does not stage cancer.

options.A: Stage explains the aim of treatment and the volume treated, which shape dose and side effects
options.B: Stage determines the beam energy used, which is the main reason the plans differ
options.C: Stage reflects how fit the patient is, which sets the number of fractions
options.D: Stage tells the therapist the exact tumour dose, which is checked against the plan each day

explanation: The correct answer is A (Stage explains the aim of treatment and the volume treated, which shape dose and side effects): Stage describes how far the cancer has spread, and it shapes the intent of treatment, curative or palliative, and the volume treated. Those in turn shape dose, fractionation and expected side effects, which is why the two plans differ. Beam energy, fitness and the prescribed dose are real parts of planning, but they are set by the oncology team and are not what stage explains. Therapists do not stage cancer, yet they need this context.

question: A newly registered radiographer on a night shift in a regional hospital reads the department incident register extract for her own shift. She notices entry 2 describes an error she caught herself before any exposure was made. The patient was unaffected. What should she do about entry 2?

options.A: Leave it unreported because no exposure was made and the patient came to no harm
options.B: Mention it informally to the colleague who booked the request and take no further action
options.C: Report it as a near miss in the incident system
options.D: Notify it as a sentinel event because a wrong-side error was involved

explanation: The correct answer is C (Report it as a near miss in the incident system): The register shows a failed process that was stopped before the exposure, which is a near miss, and near misses are reported so the system can be fixed. The Reported column reads No, so the gap is hers to close, with her supervisor told. Silence is tempting because nothing reached the patient. A sentinel event needs death or severe harm, and an informal word leaves no record.

question: An elderly inpatient arrives from a ward for a contrast CT. The radiographer asks her to state her full name and date of birth, then compares the answers with the request and wristband. The patient looks tired and says yes when asked if everything is correct. What is the best next step?

options.A: Correct the request to match what the patient said and begin the scan
options.B: Pause and resolve the date of birth discrepancy with the ward
options.C: Proceed because two of the three sources agree and the patient confirmed everything is correct
options.D: Scan the patient and send a note to the ward about the difference afterwards

explanation: The correct answer is B (Pause and resolve the date of birth discrepancy with the ward): The patient's stated date of birth differs from both the request and the wristband, so identity is not confirmed. A tired patient who agrees with a leading question is not a reliable check, and the mismatch must be resolved with the ward before contrast is given. Matching two sources feels sufficient but is not. Editing the request or acting first removes the safety check.

question: A radiographer in a busy angiography suite tells her manager she is pregnant. Her five year dosimeter record is shown. She asks whether she must stop working with radiation. The manager asks what the correct response is, given the record and the principles that apply to a declared pregnancy.

options.A: Wait until her dose approaches 20 mSv before reviewing her duties
options.B: Take no action because her five year total is comfortably within the occupational dose limit
options.C: Record the declaration, review her duties and keep foetal dose low under local policy
options.D: Move her out of all radiation work immediately because a declared pregnancy requires removal from exposure

explanation: The correct answer is C (Record the declaration, review her duties and keep foetal dose low under local policy): The record totals 17 mSv over five years, an average of 3.4 mSv, far below the 20 mSv average limit and 50 mSv single year maximum. That is not the issue, because a declared pregnancy needs a separate review of duties with foetal dose kept low under local policy. She is not banned and is not forced to disclose, so proceeding with the review is right.

question: The theatre imaging team audits how often a time-out is documented before each procedure. Results for the past twelve months are plotted. The quality coordinator asks the new practitioner on the team what the pattern means and what the team should do at this month's meeting.

options.A: Send a reminder email to staff and stop the audit to avoid reporting fatigue
options.B: Wait another quarter in case the results recover without any change
options.C: Treat the latest month as a one-off and carry on unchanged
options.D: The sustained fall since month six needs causes found, a process change and a re-audit

explanation: The correct answer is D (The sustained fall since month six needs causes found, a process change and a re-audit): The audit stayed near the 95% target to month six, then fell every month to 81%, which is a sustained trend and not random variation. The right response is to find the causes, change the process, then re-audit to check improvement. Waiting or calling it a one-off ignores the pattern, and stopping the audit removes the evidence.

question: A drowsy inpatient is brought to CT for a contrast scan. The radiographer receives the verbal handover recorded in the table. The patient cannot give a reliable history. The ward nurse is waiting to return to the ward. What should the radiographer do before proceeding with the contrast injection?

options.A: Scan without contrast first and decide on contrast only if the images are unclear
options.B: Ask the drowsy patient to confirm there are no allergies and start the scan
options.C: Proceed because the patient is stable and observations are normal
options.D: Ask the handing over nurse for the allergy status

explanation: The correct answer is D (Ask the handing over nurse for the allergy status): The Background row lists medicines and conditions but allergies are not mentioned, and an iodinated contrast injection depends on that information. The patient is drowsy, so only the nurse and record can supply it, and it should be confirmed before injecting. Normal observations do not answer the question. Dropping contrast is not the radiographer's decision to make alone.

question: A radiographer receives a notice that her continuing professional development records have been selected for audit by the Board. She reviews her log. One activity has no evidence and none of the activities cover cultural safety. How should she respond?

options.A: Supply the evidence she has, state what is missing and plan cultural safety learning
options.B: Submit the log as it stands, since the audit mainly checks that hours were completed
options.C: Withdraw the unevidenced activity from the log and submit without mentioning the gap
options.D: Report the gaps to her employer instead of the Board and let them respond

explanation: The correct answer is A (Supply the evidence she has, state what is missing and plan cultural safety learning): The log shows no evidence for the online module and no cultural safety entry, and the Board can audit both. Honest disclosure of the evidence she holds and the gaps, with a plan to fix them, is best. Submitting as is, quietly removing the entry or redirecting the matter to her employer each avoids dealing openly with the Board. Hiding a gap is a professional conduct concern in itself.

question: An 82 year old man nods often and seems unsure why he is in the department. His signed form is shown in the table. His daughter says he is fine and wants the scan started because the family is waiting. What is the best course of action for the radiographer?

options.A: Accept the signed form as valid consent and begin the scan
options.B: Hold the scan, book a qualified interpreter and reassess understanding before repeating consent
options.C: Let the daughter interpret again and have her sign as well
options.D: Proceed without contrast so that consent is not needed

explanation: The correct answer is B (Hold the scan, book a qualified interpreter and reassess understanding before repeating consent): The record shows limited English, an informal explanation by a relative, no interpreter and no capacity assessment, and the patient is nodding without clear understanding. A signed form without understanding is not valid consent. A qualified interpreter and a reassessment are needed first. Using the daughter again repeats the problem.

question: A nuclear medicine patient has been injected and is waiting. Dose rates measured around the patient are plotted. A staff member will stay at the 2 m position marked on the chart for 30 minutes while supervising the patient. What dose does she receive, and what is the best protection principle shown?

options.A: About 10 µGy, worked out as 20 µGy/h × 0.5 h
options.B: About 20 µGy, worked out as 20 µGy/h × 1 h
options.C: About 40 µGy, worked out as 80 µGy/h ÷ 2 × 1 h
options.D: About 5 µGy, worked out as 20 µGy/h × 0.25 h

explanation: The correct answer is A (About 10 µGy, worked out as 20 µGy/h × 0.5 h): The chart gives 20 µGy per hour at 2 m, which agrees with 80 ÷ 2² from the 1 m reading. Thirty minutes is 0.5 hours, so the dose is 20 × 0.5 = 10 µGy. Distance is the protection principle shown, because doubling it cuts the rate to a quarter. Reading 20 forgets the time, 40 uses inverse distance instead of the square, and 5 shortens the visit.

question: A radiographer images a 64-year-old ward patient with a portable AP chest at 100 cm SID, using manual factors of 90 kVp and 16 mAs. The department chart lists 90 kVp and 4 mAs for this size. The image is very dark, and changing the display window has not recovered the peripheral lung markings. What is the best action?

options.A: Keep the image and adjust the display window until the peripheral lung markings reappear
options.B: Repeat at 90 kVp lowered by 15 percent while keeping the original 16 mAs
options.C: Repeat once at the chart value of 4 mAs and record the deviation
options.D: Accept the image because a repeat adds dose and the heart border is clearly seen

explanation: The correct answer is C (Repeat once at the chart value of 4 mAs and record the deviation): The picture is dark with lost peripheral detail, and 16 mAs is four times the chart value of 4 mAs, so the fault is an exposure error and the image cannot answer the question. Windowing cannot add information the detector did not record. Lowering kVp by 15 percent halves the exposure to 8 mAs equivalent, still twice the chart. Accepting trades a diagnostic need for dose saved.

question: A large adult has a lateral lumbar spine on a digital detector with a grid, using 85 kVp and 20 mAs. The system reports an exposure index of 120 against a target of 400, and the vertebral detail is grainy. The department needs a repeat that reaches the target. Which mAs, at the same kVp and distance, is best?

options.A: About 67 mAs, since the detector received only 30 percent of the target exposure
options.B: Keep 20 mAs and reprocess the image with a smoother noise filter setting
options.C: About 100 mAs, five times the first exposure, to be certain of full signal
options.D: About 40 mAs, doubling the first exposure to halve the quantum noise

explanation: The correct answer is A (About 67 mAs, since the detector received only 30 percent of the target exposure): The index of 120 against a target of 400 is a ratio of 0.30 (a deviation index of about −5). The needed mAs is 20 ÷ 0.30 = 67. Doubling to 40 mAs gives an index near 240, still well under target. 100 mAs gives about 600, an unnecessary overexposure. Reprocessing cannot repair quantum mottle.

question: A 34-year-old man with a three week cough and a possible upper lobe lesion has an erect PA chest on a wall stand detector. Breath hold and exposure factors were correct, but the lung apices are not included on the image. The referrer specifically asked about the upper zones. What is the best action?

options.A: Repeat with the beam angled 15° caudally so the apices project into the field
options.B: Repeat with wider collimation and a lower kVp to improve contrast at the lung tops
options.C: Repeat with the detector raised above the shoulders and the same factors
options.D: Accept the image and ask the radiologist to comment, since apical lesions are rarely missed

explanation: The correct answer is C (Repeat with the detector raised above the shoulders and the same factors): The image has the top of the field cut off, so the apices the referrer asked about are missing. The question cannot be answered, so repeating is justified. The cause is receptor position, so raising the detector fixes it with unchanged factors. Angling or changing kVp does not bring missing anatomy into the field.

question: A four-year-old with a suspected finger injury has a PA hand exposed at 100 mA for 0.16 s, giving 16 mAs. The parent steadied the hand while wearing a lead apron, but the image is blurred and the phalanges are unclear. Which technique change best prevents this on the repeat?

options.A: Add an 8:1 grid and double the mAs to sharpen the bone edges
options.B: Keep the same exposure and rely on the parent to hold the fingers flat by hand
options.C: Use 50 mA with 0.32 s to lower the tube load for the small hand
options.D: Use 200 mA with 0.08 s to keep 16 mAs, and immobilise with a foam pad

explanation: The correct answer is D (Use 200 mA with 0.08 s to keep 16 mAs, and immobilise with a foam pad): The picture shows motion blur. Motion unsharpness falls with a shorter exposure time, so use a higher mA and shorter time to keep the same mAs: 200 mA × 0.08 s = 16 mAs. Immobilisation devices come before hand holding. A longer time worsens blur, and a grid raises dose with no gain on a small part.

question: A seven-year-old with a twisted knee has a lateral knee radiograph taken with the adult knee technique and the grid left in place. The image is dark with poor bone detail, and the exposure index is well above target. Which approach is best for the repeat?

options.A: Keep the adult factors but move the tube to 200 cm to lower the entrance dose
options.B: Use the paediatric protocol without the grid, with tight collimation and short time
options.C: Keep the grid and halve the mAs, because a small knee produces little scatter
options.D: Keep the adult factors and place a lead shield over the knee to reduce dose

explanation: The correct answer is B (Use the paediatric protocol without the grid, with tight collimation and short time): The picture is dark because adult factors and a grid overexposed a small knee. Adult settings can overexpose a small child, so a protocol for size or age is used, the grid is removed for small parts and the field is tight. A shield over the knee would obscure the area of interest, and keeping the grid or adult factors leaves the error.

question: A 71-year-old man in pain with suspected bowel obstruction has a supine AP abdomen on a trolley. The exposure time was 0.4 s during quiet breathing, and the gas pattern is blurred. The doctor asks whether the film is usable. What is the best action?

options.A: Repeat with the mAs doubled at the same time, to sharpen the bowel gas
options.B: Accept the film because the gas pattern is partly visible and a repeat adds dose
options.C: Tell the doctor the film is unusable and recommend CT instead of repeating the radiograph
options.D: Repeat once on suspended expiration with the shortest time, and record the cause

explanation: The correct answer is D (Repeat once on suspended expiration with the shortest time, and record the cause): The picture shows motion blur across the gas pattern, so the question cannot be answered from it. A repeat on suspended expiration with a short time addresses breathing motion, and recording the cause feeds reject analysis. More mAs does not reduce blur. Recommending CT skips a simple repeat that is within the radiographer's scope.

question: A portable AP pelvis on a trolley is taken at 100 cm SID with 20 mAs and a focused 8:1 grid whose focal range is 150 to 180 cm. The image is adequately dark in the centre but clearly lighter toward both lateral edges. What is the best repeat technique?

options.A: Flip the grid so the lead strips face the other way and expose at 100 cm
options.B: Repeat at 150 cm SID, inside the grid's focal range, raising mAs to about 45
options.C: Repeat at 150 cm SID and keep 20 mAs, since the grid will now work correctly
options.D: Repeat at 100 cm SID with the central ray moved to the centre of the grid

explanation: The correct answer is B (Repeat at 150 cm SID, inside the grid's focal range, raising mAs to about 45): Density falling at both edges with a normal centre is off-focus cutoff: the SID is outside the grid's range. Moving to 150 cm fixes it, and the mAs must rise by (150 ÷ 100)² = 2.25, so 20 × 2.25 = 45 mAs. Keeping 20 mAs gives about 44 percent of the signal. Decentring or a reversed grid produce different patterns.

question: A 45-year-old man with suspected left ureteric colic has a supine AP abdomen. The detector was placed crosswise but sat too far toward his right side, and his left flank is missing from the image. Exposure factors were correct. What is the best action?

options.A: Repeat with the detector and central ray centred on the midline so both flanks are included
options.B: Crop and rotate the image digitally so the missing left flank is brought back into view
options.C: Accept the image and write in the examination notes that the left flank is not shown
options.D: Repeat with the beam angled laterally toward the left flank to project it onto the detector

explanation: The correct answer is A (Repeat with the detector and central ray centred on the midline so both flanks are included): The right edge of the image, which is the patient's left side, is cut off, and the history asks about the left ureter. Missing anatomy cannot be recovered by processing. The cause is detector position, so the fix is to centre detector and beam. Angling the tube would distort rather than include the flank.

question: A 55-year-old with bilateral hand pain after a crush injury has both hands imaged on a busy shift. Neither PA hand image carries a side marker, and the radiographer cannot recall which hand was exposed first. The worklist lists both hands. What should happen next?

options.A: Repeat both hands with a marker in the beam, since neither side is certain
options.B: Repeat only the hand with more swelling and label the other from the worklist order
options.C: Accept the images and ask the radiologist to decide the side from the bone anatomy
options.D: Add a digital marker to each image using the order of the worklist entries

explanation: The correct answer is A (Repeat both hands with a marker in the beam, since neither side is certain): The picture has no side marker anywhere, and neither the image nor the record settles which hand it is. A wrong side can drive surgical planning, so a side must never be guessed or digitally added when it is not certain. Both images are therefore unsafe, and both hands need a repeat with the marker in the beam.

question: Using the department technique chart for an adult AP abdomen of 22 cm, a radiographer must use 130 cm SID because of overhead equipment. The grid's focal range includes 130 cm and the kVp stays at 75. Which mAs keeps the detector signal unchanged?

options.A: About 12 mAs, since a longer distance concentrates the beam on the detector
options.B: About 80 mAs, since the grid factor must be applied again at the new distance
options.C: About 34 mAs, since the inverse square law cuts the intensity to roughly 59 percent
options.D: About 26 mAs, since mAs rises in direct proportion to the distance ratio

explanation: The correct answer is C (About 34 mAs, since the inverse square law cuts the intensity to roughly 59 percent): The chart gives 20 mAs at 100 cm with an 8:1 grid. New mAs = 20 × (130 ÷ 100)² = 20 × 1.69 = 33.8, about 34 mAs. The linear answer is 26, the inverted answer is 11.8, and 80 mAs would repeat the grid factor of 4 already built into the chart value.

question: A chest room's exposure index log is shown for six consecutive days using the same AEC settings and a target index of 400. Every image was reported as diagnostic, and the department accepts a deviation index within ±1. What is the best response?

options.A: Repeat the days with a deviation index above 1 to restore on-target doses
options.B: Take no action until an image is rejected for looking too dark
options.C: Raise the target exposure index to 600 so the log returns to zero deviation
options.D: Audit technique and AEC settings, because the steady rise suggests dose creep

explanation: The correct answer is D (Audit technique and AEC settings, because the steady rise suggests dose creep): The index climbs every day and the deviation index passes +1 on day 4 and reaches +2.4, while the images still look fine. That pattern is dose creep, found only by checking the index. Repeating adds dose for no benefit, and raising the target hides the drift. The cause is found by auditing technique and AEC settings.

question: A service audits its adult examinations against the reference levels it has adopted for each examination, as shown in the table of median doses. The manager asks what the figures mean for practice and which response fits the department's duty to optimise doses. Which response is best?

options.A: Take no action, because reference levels apply to individual patients, not a service's typical dose
options.B: Suspend AP abdomen examinations until the median DAP falls below the reference level, a legal limit
options.C: Investigate AP abdomen technique, since its typical dose exceeds the benchmark
options.D: Review the PA chest first because its median sits furthest below the reference level

explanation: The correct answer is C (Investigate AP abdomen technique, since its typical dose exceeds the benchmark): Only the AP abdomen median (3.1 Gy·cm²) exceeds its reference level (2.5). A reference level is a benchmark for typical doses, so exceeding it triggers investigation and optimisation, not suspension. The chest, lumbar spine and pelvis are below their levels and need no urgent action. Reference levels judge a service's typical dose, not one patient.

question: A reject audit for three computed radiography rooms is shown for one month, with every cause recorded by the operator at the time of rejection. The audit lead asks which action should come first for Room 3, which has the highest reject rate. Which action is best?

options.A: Increase the exposure factors in Room 3 to overcome the line seen on the images
options.B: Withdraw CR plate 7 from use, test or clean it, then recheck the room's reject rate
options.C: Arrange positioning training for Room 3 staff, since it has the most rejected images
options.D: Recalibrate the exposure index for all detectors in the department

explanation: The correct answer is B (Withdraw CR plate 7 from use, test or clean it, then recheck the room's reject rate): Room 3 has 71 rejects from 440 images (16.1 percent), and its recorded cause is the same line on images from one plate. A repeating mark from a single plate means dust or a scratch, so the plate is removed and cleaned or retired. Training and extra exposure do not remove a plate defect, and other rooms show no such pattern.

question: The morning list is shown. The 0915 patient attends for an AP pelvis after a fall. She tells the radiographer her period is a week late and she has not had a pregnancy test. Which action is best before any exposure?

options.A: Proceed with the exposure and place a lead apron over the abdomen to protect the foetus
options.B: Ask the patient to sign that she accepts the foetal risk, then proceed with the exposure
options.C: Hold the exposure and discuss the possible pregnancy with the referrer first
options.D: Proceed with the exposure and record the late period in the notes for the radiologist

explanation: The correct answer is C (Hold the exposure and discuss the possible pregnancy with the referrer first): The alert row shows a late period and no pregnancy test, and the examination irradiates the pelvis. For a possible pregnancy the practitioner neither simply proceeds nor simply refuses; the referrer reconsiders justification first. Shielding does not meaningfully reduce dose, and consent does not replace a justification review.

question: A CT list is checked against a local protocol that accepts an eGFR result up to 30 days old and requires the radiologist to be told before injection when the eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². Which patient needs that step before cannulation?

options.A: Patient 4, because the eGFR of 27 is below 30 and the result is current
options.B: Patient 2, because the eGFR of 61 and metformin use need review before injection
options.C: Patient 3, because the eGFR of 34 sits near the protocol point of 30
options.D: Patient 5, because the eGFR of 45 together with metformin use needs review first

explanation: The correct answer is A (Patient 4, because the eGFR of 27 is below 30 and the result is current): Only patient 4 has an eGFR (27) below the protocol point of 30, and the result is only 5 days old, so the radiologist is told before cannulation. Metformin decisions follow local protocol and the radiologist, not the radiographer's own judgement. Patient 3 at 34 is above the point, however close it looks. Patients 2 and 5 take metformin but have eGFRs of 61 and 45.

question: During a mobile examination, the scatter dose rate at 1 m from the patient is taken as 100 percent. The radiographer wants to stand where the rate is 10 percent or less. The chart shows the dose rate against distance. Where should the radiographer stand?

options.A: At 2 m, because doubling the distance halves the dose rate
options.B: At about 3.2 m or further, where the curve reaches the 10 percent line
options.C: At 10 m, because a tenth of the dose rate needs ten times the distance
options.D: At 3 m, the nearest whole metre to where the curve meets the line

explanation: The correct answer is B (At about 3.2 m or further, where the curve reaches the 10 percent line): Dose rate ∝ 1 ÷ d², so 10 percent needs d = √10 = 3.16 m. At 3 m the rate is 100 ÷ 9 = 11 percent, still above the line. At 2 m it is 25 percent, not 50. At 10 m it would be 1 percent, far more distance than needed.

question: A knee is exposed at 70 kVp and 24 mAs. The radiographer raises the kVp to 80 and wants the same detector signal. The chart shows relative detector exposure at constant mAs. The patient is an adult of average build. Which mAs and effect are correct?

options.A: About 24 mAs, since kVp changes only contrast and does not alter detector signal
options.B: About 6 mAs, with a lower patient dose and slightly higher image contrast
options.C: About 12 mAs, with a lower patient dose and slightly lower image contrast
options.D: About 47 mAs, with a higher patient dose and slightly higher image contrast

explanation: The correct answer is C (About 12 mAs, with a lower patient dose and slightly lower image contrast): The curve reads about 1.9 at 80 kVp, so the detector exposure nearly doubles at constant mAs. Required mAs = 24 ÷ 1.94 = 12.4, about 12. Less mAs means lower patient dose, and higher kVp lowers contrast. Multiplying gives 47. Leaving 24 mAs would overexpose, and 6 mAs would underexpose.

question: A department reviews its digital detector response curve. A chest image was taken at four times the target detector exposure, and the display looks acceptable to the radiographer, who is unaware of the setting error. Which statement is best supported by the curve?

options.A: It lies within the working range, so the exposure is acceptable and needs no follow up
options.B: The curve shows pixel values fall as exposure rises, so a darker image signals overexposure
options.C: It lies beyond saturation, so the image would be obviously white and rejected at once
options.D: It lies within the working range, so the image can look normal at four times target

explanation: The correct answer is D (It lies within the working range, so the image can look normal at four times target): Four times target is log10(4) = 0.6 on the horizontal axis, where the pixel value is far below saturation. The detector still records the image, so the computer can display it normally even though the exposure is four times target (a deviation index of about +6). Working range is not the same as an acceptable exposure.

question: On a chest examination a radiographer used 12 mAs, giving an exposure index of 600 against a target of 400, and the image looked fine. The chart shows exposure index against mAs for this room at the same kVp and distance. What mAs should the next patient of similar size receive?

options.A: 12 mAs again, because the image looked acceptable
options.B: 6 mAs, half the first exposure, to halve the dose again
options.C: 4 mAs, a third of the first exposure, to keep the dose very low
options.D: About 8 mAs, where the line meets the target of 400

explanation: The correct answer is D (About 8 mAs, where the line meets the target of 400): On the line, the index is 50 per mAs, so the target of 400 is reached at 400 ÷ 50 = 8 mAs. At 6 mAs the index is 300 (deviation index −1.2), outside the accepted band, and 4 mAs gives 200 (−3.0). Repeating 12 mAs keeps the index at 600 (+1.8).

question: A colleague suggests removing the 1 mm of added aluminium filtration from a general room to raise the detector signal because the images seem slightly pale. The chart models relative skin dose and detector signal against added filtration. What is the best response?

options.A: Agree, because removing filtration lowers skin dose while raising the detector signal
options.B: Decline, since removal cuts detector signal by 42 percent and raises skin dose 5 percent
options.C: Agree, because the extra signal would let the mAs be halved and the dose fall
options.D: Decline, since removal raises skin dose about 42 percent for only 5 percent more signal

explanation: The correct answer is D (Decline, since removal raises skin dose about 42 percent for only 5 percent more signal): At 1 mm the chart reads skin dose 70.5 and signal 95.1. At 0 mm both are 100. Skin dose therefore rises by 100 ÷ 70.5 = 1.42, about 42 percent, while signal rises by only 100 ÷ 95.1 = 1.05, about 5 percent. Filtration removes low energy photons that add skin dose but little to the image.

question: In a Hobart hot lab, a Tc-99m vial was calibrated at 1,100 MBq at 07:00. A late-list bone scan needs 300 MBq in the syringe at the moment of injection. The technologist plots the vial decay as percent of starting activity against hours after 07:00. What is the latest clock time the vial can still supply this dose?

options.A: About 18:15, worked out as 6.01 h × log2(1,100 ÷ 300)
options.B: About 13:00, worked out as 1 half-life of 6 h after 07:00
options.C: About 15:45, worked out as 12 h × 800 ÷ 1,100 after 07:00
options.D: About 19:00, worked out as 2 half-lives of 6 h after 07:00

explanation: The correct answer is A (About 18:15, worked out as 6.01 h × log2(1,100 ÷ 300)): The required fraction is 300 ÷ 1,100 = 27.3 percent of the calibrated activity. Tc-99m has a half-life of 6.01 hours, so t = 6.01 × log2(1 ÷ 0.273) = 11.3 hours, which is about 18:15 and where the curve crosses the dashed line. After one half-life the vial still holds 550 MBq, so stopping there wastes a usable vial. A straight line ignores exponential decay, and two half-lives leave only 275 MBq, which is slightly too little.

question: At a Darwin PET centre one F-18 FDG vial, calibrated at 08:00, must cover three booked patients, and the next delivery arrives after 14:00. The table lists each patient's prescribed activity beside the activity an untouched vial would hold at that slot. Early on, the technologist reviews the list. What is the best action?

options.A: Draw the whole remaining vial for the 13:00 patient and lengthen the acquisition time to compensate
options.B: Scale the 13:00 dose down to the vial's remaining activity and record it as prescribed
options.C: Tell the physician the vial cannot supply the 13:00 dose, then arrange another vial or slot
options.D: Draw 2.0 mL for the 13:00 patient using the concentration printed on the delivery label

explanation: The correct answer is C (Tell the physician the vial cannot supply the 13:00 dose, then arrange another vial or slot): Decay-corrected activity falls to about 181 MBq by 13:00, well under the 400 MBq prescribed for a 99 kg patient. Even the 11:15 patient is at risk, because after 270 MBq is drawn at 09:30 only about 211 MBq would remain by 11:15 against 330 MBq prescribed. Only the physician can accept a changed activity, so the supply gap must be reported and a new vial or slot arranged. A low dose with longer imaging, an edited prescription, or a volume from the 08:00 label each give the wrong activity.

question: A six year old girl with a dilated right renal pelvis on ultrasound has a Tc-99m MAG3 study in a Melbourne children's hospital. Furosemide was given at 15 minutes when the pelvis was full, as protocol requires. The chart shows both kidneys. The nuclear medicine physician is in the department. What is the best action?

options.A: Give a second furosemide dose straight away to see whether the right curve then falls
options.B: Report the right system as baggy but unobstructed, because furosemide was given at the correct time
options.C: Mark the study non-diagnostic because a curve failed to fall, and rebook the child
options.D: Show the physician the right kidney curve and the furosemide time before the child leaves

explanation: The correct answer is D (Show the physician the right kidney curve and the furosemide time before the child leaves): The left curve peaks early and falls, and falls faster after furosemide, while the right curve keeps rising and stays flat after the diuretic at 15 minutes. That pattern is a result for the physician to interpret, not a technical failure. A technologist does not report a diagnosis, add medicine on their own, or discard a valid study. The time of the diuretic is part of what the physician needs.

question: At 07:45 in a Perth nuclear medicine department, the technologist logs the daily Cs-137 constancy check on the dose calibrator. A bone scan patient is booked for 08:30 and the syringe is ready in its pot. The week's log is in the table, with a department tolerance of plus or minus 5 percent. What is the best action?

options.A: Repeat the reading with the source reseated, check for chamber contamination, and hold patient doses
options.B: Carry on with today's list and repeat the test at the next scheduled accuracy check
options.C: Apply a correction factor of 1.13 to each dose reading taken today and carry on
options.D: Compare Thursday with Wednesday alone and accept the small change as normal day to day drift

explanation: The correct answer is A (Repeat the reading with the source reseated, check for chamber contamination, and hold patient doses): Thursday reads 6.55 MBq against 7.40 MBq expected, a deviation of 11.5 percent, outside the plus or minus 5 percent tolerance after three days within about half a percent. The first response is to repeat with the source reseated and check for chamber contamination. Patient doses are not measured on the calibrator until it passes. A correction factor, a later test or calling it drift all leave an unproven instrument in use.

question: A Tc-99m generator in a Cairns hospital is eluted each morning. On Monday afternoon a second elution is needed for an urgent lung scan, and the log shows far less activity than the morning yield. A junior colleague wants to quarantine the generator for a failed column. The elution log is in the table. What is the best response?

options.A: Treat the low yield as Mo-99 breakthrough and discard the eluate without testing
options.B: Six hours of ingrowth gives about half a full yield, so the eluate is usable
options.C: Agree the column is failing, quarantine the generator, and order a replacement from the supplier
options.D: Elute again straight away to collect the missing Tc-99m left on the column

explanation: The correct answer is B (Six hours of ingrowth gives about half a full yield, so the eluate is usable): After an elution, Tc-99m grows back from Mo-99 and peaks about 23 hours later. At six hours the yield is only about half of the 24 hour figure, here 8,775 against 18,400 MBq, so the log is what ingrowth predicts. A failing column would not be judged from the interval alone. A repeat elution gives even less, and breakthrough is tested by the purity check, not inferred from yield.

question: At 07:30 in a Sydney private practice, the single-head gamma camera has its daily checks recorded in the table, and the first patient is a Tc-99m bone scan at 08:00. Nobody changed the camera settings since yesterday, and the energy window is still set on 140 keV with a 20 percent width. What is the best action?

options.A: Scan the patient because 131 keV still falls inside the 126 to 154 keV window
options.B: Repeat the energy peaking to centre the window on the photopeak, then repeat the flood test
options.C: Widen the window to 30 percent so the shifted photopeak sits comfortably inside it
options.D: Scan the patient and correct the counts with software after the study is finished

explanation: The correct answer is B (Repeat the energy peaking to centre the window on the photopeak, then repeat the flood test): A 20 percent window on 140 keV runs from 126 to 154 keV, so 131 keV is inside it but the window is no longer centred on the photopeak, which loses true counts and changes the flood. The camera should be re-peaked and the flood repeated before any patient. A wider window lets in more scatter and lowers contrast, and fixing the data afterwards by software does not restore a mis-centred window.

question: A 58 year old with diabetes has a Tc-99m egg meal gastric emptying study at a Brisbane hospital, imaged hourly for four hours. Her arrival glucose was 17.8 mmol/L and the meal and times followed protocol. The retention curve is plotted. The technologist has already noted her medicines. What is the best action?

options.A: Send the curve alone, because glucose is a patient factor and not a technical one
options.B: Report delayed gastric emptying as confirmed because retention is still high at four hours
options.C: Discard the curve and repeat the study today with a second meal and fresh tracer
options.D: Send the curve with the arrival glucose and medicines so the physician can interpret emptying

explanation: The correct answer is D (Send the curve with the arrival glucose and medicines so the physician can interpret emptying): Uncontrolled blood glucose and some medicines change gastric emptying, so the 17.8 mmol/L result and the medicines must travel with the curve. The meal and imaging times were correct, so the study is valid and the physician decides how to interpret it. Reporting a diagnosis is outside scope, and an immediate repeat gives avoidable radiation with the same glucose. Sending the curve without the context hides the cause.

question: A patient in a shielded ward in Adelaide received I-131 for thyroid cancer. The bedside reading is 24 µSv/h at 1 m. A staff member must stay near the patient for a short task and wants the dose rate no higher than 6 µSv/h. The rate was plotted for each distance. Where should the staff member stand?

options.A: 2 m, worked out as 1 m × √(24 ÷ 6)
options.B: 4 m, worked out as 1 m × (24 ÷ 6)
options.C: 16 m, worked out as 1 m × (24 ÷ 6)²
options.D: 0.5 m, worked out as 1 m × √(6 ÷ 24)

explanation: The correct answer is A (2 m, worked out as 1 m × √(24 ÷ 6)): Dose rate follows the inverse square law, so the distance scales with the square root of the rate ratio: 1 m × √(24 ÷ 6) = 2 m. At 2 m the rate is 24 ÷ 4 = 6 µSv/h, which is where the plotted curve meets the target line. Treating the fall as inversely proportional to distance gives 4 m. Squaring the ratio gives 16 m, and inverting the ratio gives 0.5 m, a point closer to the patient where the rate is higher.

question: In a Darwin hot lab a vial of Tc-99m tipped over. Others were warned, the area is cordoned off and the spill is covered with absorbent paper. The technologist, who had a splash on one sleeve, surveys with a Geiger-Muller meter. Background is 60 counts per second. The results are tabulated. What is the best next step?

options.A: Clean the floor next, because other staff will walk across it before the hand matters
options.B: Remove coat and gloves into waste, wash hand gently with lukewarm water and soap, resurvey
options.C: Leave everything in place until the Tc-99m has decayed, then survey the hand again
options.D: Scrub the hand with a stiff brush and strong detergent until the reading drops

explanation: The correct answer is B (Remove coat and gloves into waste, wash hand gently with lukewarm water and soap, resurvey): The hand reads 450 counts per second against an action level of 180, and the sleeve reads 1,900, so the person is contaminated and comes first. Contaminated clothing and gloves go into radioactive waste, then the skin is washed gently with lukewarm water and mild soap and resurveyed. Hard scrubbing can break the skin and drive activity in. The floor at 320 is also over the level but can follow, and waiting for decay leaves the skin exposed for hours.

question: A rural Queensland department checks dose calibrator linearity by decaying a Tc-99m source over two days. The department tolerance is plus or minus 10 percent, and a high activity therapy dose is due to be measured this afternoon. The results are tabulated. The calibrator is the only one on site. What is the best action?

options.A: Leave the calibrator in use and repeat linearity at the next scheduled interval
options.B: Accept the result because every reading except the first is within tolerance
options.C: Report the failed linearity and stop using this calibrator for the high activity dose
options.D: Apply the top reading's deviation as a correction factor to the therapy dose and proceed

explanation: The correct answer is C (Report the failed linearity and stop using this calibrator for the high activity dose): At 22,000 MBq the instrument reads 13.8 percent low, outside the 10 percent tolerance, while the lower readings pass. Linearity shows whether the reading stays proportional across the range, so the high activity end cannot be trusted and a therapy dose lies there. The failed result goes to the person responsible for equipment and the calibrator is not used for that dose until corrected. A correction factor, acceptance of the other readings or a delayed repeat each rely on an unproven reading.

question: A whole body probe measures retention in a patient treated with I-131, whose physical half-life is about 8 days.
